title: True to the self or stuck in delay? Authenticity moderates the associations between perfectionism and procrastination
abstract: Background Perfectionism has long been linked to procrastination, yet findings remain mixed, suggesting that high standards may facilitate or hinder action depending on whether they are accompanied by self-critical concerns. Authenticity may be related to how discrepancies between standards and performance are construed. The present study examined whether authenticity moderates the associations of adaptive and maladaptive perfectionism with procrastination and whether maladaptive perfectionism shows a necessary-condition pattern. Participants and procedure The sample consisted of 300 adults who completed an anonymous online survey. Perfectionism was assessed using the Polish Adaptive and Maladaptive Perfectionism Questionnaire, procrastination with the Pure Procrastination Scale, and authenticity with the Authenticity Inventory-3, operationalized as a global manifest score. Data were analyzed using multiple regression models and necessary condition analysis (NCA). Results Maladaptive perfectionism was positively associated with procrastination, whereas adaptive perfectionism was negatively associated. NCA yielded moderate but symmetric necessity and sufficiency effects, which did not support a genuine necessary condition. Authenticity moderated both relationships: at higher authenticity, the positive association of maladaptive perfectionism with procrastination was weaker, whereas the negative association of adaptive perfectionism was stronger. Conclusions Maladaptive perfectionism was positively associated with procrastination, whereas adaptive perfectionism was inversely associated with it. The strength of these associations varied with authenticity, although the moderation effects were modest. This pattern is consistent with the discrepancy-processing account. The symmetric NCA pattern indicated a constrained distribution rather than a genuine necessary condition.
